solution:
The IUPAC definition of a transition element is a metal having an incompletely filled \(d\) subshell either in the neutral atom OR in any of its common oxidation states — the ground state alone does not settle it.

Silver is \([\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^{1}\), so in the ground state the \(d\) subshell is indeed full. However silver also exhibits the \(+2\) state (for example in \(\text{AgF}_2\) and \(\text{AgO}\)), and

\(\text{Ag}^{2+} = [\text{Kr}]4d^{9}\)

which has an incompletely filled \(4d\) subshell.

Because silver has a stable oxidation state with a partly filled \(d\) subshell, it is classified as a transition element.

The enthalpy of atomisation measures the strength of the metallic bonding, and metallic bonding in the transition series is strong because BOTH the \((n-1)d\) and the \(ns\) electrons take part in it. The more unpaired \(d\) electrons an atom has, the stronger the interatomic interaction.

Zinc is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{2}\). Its \(3d\) subshell is completely filled, so there are no unpaired \(d\) electrons and the \(3d\) electrons are not available for metallic bonding — only the two \(4s\) electrons are. Every other member of the series from Sc to Cu has at least one unpaired \(3d\) electron contributing to the bonding.

With the weakest interatomic bonding in the series, zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation, \(126\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (The same cause gives zinc the lowest melting and boiling points of the series.)

Manganese, \(Z = 25\), exhibits the largest number of oxidation states: \(+2, +3, +4, +5, +6\) and \(+7\).

Reason: its ground-state configuration is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{2}\), which has the maximum number of unpaired electrons in the series — five in \(3d\) plus the \(4s\) pair. All seven of these electrons lie in orbitals of comparable energy and can therefore be lost or shared, so every oxidation state from \(+2\) (both \(4s\) electrons lost) up to \(+7\) (all seven lost, as in \(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\)) is accessible.

Elements at the two ends of the series are restricted either by having too few electrons to lose (Sc, Ti) or by having their \(d\) electrons too tightly paired and held (Cu, Zn).

Manganese.

\(E^{\circ}(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M})\) is fixed by the balance of three terms in the cycle

\(\text{M(s)} \rightarrow \text{M(g)} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\)

namely the enthalpy of atomisation \(\Delta_a H^{\circ}\), the sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies \((\Delta_i H_1 + \Delta_i H_2)\), and the hydration enthalpy \(\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H^{\circ}\). Only the last is negative and it is the term that pays for the first two.

For copper the two energy-consuming steps are unusually expensive — it has a high enthalpy of atomisation and a high sum of ionisation enthalpies — while the hydration enthalpy of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) is not negative enough to compensate them. The overall \(\Delta G^{\circ}\) for \(\text{Cu(s)} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\) is therefore positive, so the reverse (reduction) is spontaneous and \(E^{\circ}\) comes out positive, \(+0.34\,\text{V}\).

The chemical consequence is that copper cannot reduce \(\text{H}^{+}\): it does not liberate \(\text{H}_2\) from acids, and it dissolves only in oxidising acids such as nitric or hot concentrated sulphuric acid.

The variation is irregular because the ionisation enthalpy depends not only on the steadily increasing nuclear charge but also on the stability of the electronic configuration LEFT BEHIND in the ion, and \(d^{0}\), \(d^{5}\) and \(d^{10}\) configurations are exceptionally stable.

First ionisation enthalpy: a \(4s\) electron is removed. The increase across the series is only slight and irregular, because the \(3d\) electrons being added screen the \(4s\) electrons from the rising nuclear charge fairly effectively, so the two effects nearly cancel.

Second ionisation enthalpy: a \(3d\) electron is removed, and here the configuration effect is large and shows up as clear breaks —

- Cr is anomalously HIGH, because \(\text{Cr}^{+}\) is \(3d^{5}\) and the electron has to be taken out of a stable half-filled subshell;
- Cu is anomalously HIGH, because \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) is \(3d^{10}\), a stable completely filled subshell;
- Mn is anomalously LOW, because removal gives \(\text{Mn}^{2+} = 3d^{5}\), the extra-stable half-filled configuration.

So the irregular variation of the first and second ionisation enthalpies is attributed to the differing stabilities of the \(3d\) configurations of the resulting ions, superimposed on the general rise in effective nuclear charge.

Reaching the highest oxidation state of a metal means removing or sharing the largest possible number of electrons, and only a very small, very electronegative and strongly oxidising partner can do that.

Oxygen and fluorine are the two smallest and most electronegative elements. Their small size allows a large number of them to be packed around one metal atom (a high coordination number), and their high electronegativity lets them draw the metal to its extreme oxidation state.

Oxygen is superior to fluorine for this purpose because, besides the \(\sigma\) bond, it can form \(p\pi-d\pi\) MULTIPLE bonds to the metal using its lone pairs and the metal's empty \(d\) orbitals. It therefore stabilises the highest state with fewer atoms. This is why the highest manganese fluoride is \(\text{MnF}_4\) whereas the highest oxide is \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7\), and why the \(+7\) state appears in \(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\).

Hence the highest oxidation state of a metal is exhibited in its oxide (or oxoanion) or fluoride only.

\(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) is the stronger reducing agent.

A reducing agent is itself oxidised, so compare what each ion becomes on losing one electron. Both start from an aqueous, weak-field (high-spin) octahedral environment:

\(\text{Cr}^{2+}(d^{4}) \rightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+}(d^{3})\)

\(\text{Fe}^{2+}(d^{6}) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}(d^{5})\)

Oxidation of \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) produces \(d^{3}\), which in an octahedral field is \(t_{2g}^{3}\) — a half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level with the maximum crystal-field stabilisation energy available to a high-spin ion. That is a large driving force, so \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) gives up its electron readily.

Oxidation of \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) produces \(d^{5}\), which is \(t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}\) in a weak field and therefore has ZERO crystal-field stabilisation energy. Its only advantage is the half-filled \(3d\) subshell, a far weaker incentive.

The electrode potentials confirm it: \(E^{\circ}(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+}) \approx -0.41\,\text{V}\) (strongly negative, so oxidation is easy) against \(E^{\circ}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) \approx +0.77\,\text{V}\) (positive, so \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) resists oxidation and \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) is in fact an oxidising agent).

\(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) is the stronger reducing agent.

\(Z = 27\) is cobalt, \([\text{Ar}]3d^{7}4s^{2}\). A transition metal loses its \(ns\) electrons before the \((n-1)d\) electrons, so

\(\text{Co}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{7}\)

Distributing seven electrons over the five \(3d\) orbitals by Hund's rule in the weak (high-spin) aqueous field gives two doubly-occupied and three singly-occupied orbitals, so the number of unpaired electrons is

\(n = 3\)

Spin-only formula:

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15}\)

\(\mu = 3.87\,\text{BM}\)

Because in water \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) disproportionates — it is simultaneously oxidised and reduced:

\(2\text{Cu}^{+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\)

The reason is a hydration effect. Removing a second electron from \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) is expensive, since \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) is \(3d^{10}\) and the second ionisation enthalpy of copper is high. But \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) is smaller and doubly charged, so its hydration enthalpy is very much more negative than that of \(\text{Cu}^{+}\), and that difference more than pays for the second ionisation enthalpy.

The overall \(\Delta G^{\circ}\) for the disproportionation is therefore negative (the cell reaction is favourable, \(E^{\circ} \approx +0.38\,\text{V}\)), so \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) cannot survive in aqueous solution.

Copper(I) is consequently known only in the solid state or as insoluble/complexed species — \(\text{Cu}_2\text{O}\), CuCl, CuI — where hydration cannot drive the disproportionation.

Both contractions have the same cause — the imperfect shielding of one \(f\) electron by another — but \(5f\) orbitals shield even more poorly than \(4f\) orbitals do.

The \(5f\) orbitals are more diffuse and extend further from the nucleus than the \(4f\) orbitals of the corresponding lanthanoid, so they penetrate the core less and screen the outer electrons less effectively. As each proton is added along the actinoid series, a larger fraction of that added nuclear charge is actually felt by the outer electrons.

The effective nuclear charge therefore rises more steeply from element to element in the actinoids than in the lanthanoids, and the size shrinks correspondingly more per element.

Hence the actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than the lanthanoid contraction.

In every case the \(ns\) electrons are removed before the \((n-1)d\) electrons, and for the \(f\)-block the \(ns\) and then the \((n-1)d\) electrons go before the \((n-2)f\) electrons.

(i) Cr (\(Z = 24\)) is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}\), so \(\text{Cr}^{3+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{3}\)

(ii) Pm (\(Z = 61\)) is \([\text{Xe}]4f^{5}6s^{2}\), so \(\text{Pm}^{3+} = [\text{Xe}]4f^{4}\)

(iii) Cu (\(Z = 29\)) is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}\), so \(\text{Cu}^{+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{10}\)

(iv) Ce (\(Z = 58\)) is \([\text{Xe}]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}\), so \(\text{Ce}^{4+} = [\text{Xe}]\) (i.e. \(4f^{0}\), a noble-gas core — which is why \(\text{Ce}^{4+}\) is so well known)

(v) Co (\(Z = 27\)) is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{7}4s^{2}\), so \(\text{Co}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{7}\)

(vi) Lu (\(Z = 71\)) is \([\text{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^{1}6s^{2}\), so \(\text{Lu}^{2+} = [\text{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^{1}\)

(vii) Mn (\(Z = 25\)) is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{2}\), so \(\text{Mn}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{5}\)

(viii) Th (\(Z = 90\)) is \([\text{Rn}]6d^{2}7s^{2}\), so \(\text{Th}^{4+} = [\text{Rn}]\) (i.e. \(5f^{0}\))

Compare the configuration each ion would have to give up in going to the \(+3\) state.

\(\text{Mn}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{5}\), a half-filled \(3d\) subshell, which carries extra exchange-energy stability. Oxidising it to \(\text{Mn}^{3+} = 3d^{4}\) DESTROYS that stability, so the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese is exceptionally high and the oxidation is difficult.

\(\text{Fe}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{6}\). Oxidising it to \(\text{Fe}^{3+} = 3d^{5}\) CREATES the stable half-filled configuration, so the third ionisation enthalpy of iron is comparatively low and the oxidation is easy.

The electrode potentials show the same thing: \(E^{\circ}(\text{Mn}^{3+}/\text{Mn}^{2+}) \approx +1.5\,\text{V}\) (so \(\text{Mn}^{3+}\) is strongly oxidising and reverts to \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\)) against \(E^{\circ}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) \approx +0.77\,\text{V}\).

Hence \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) compounds are more stable than \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) compounds towards oxidation to the \(+3\) state.

The \(+2\) state is reached by losing the two \(4s\) electrons. Whether it is STABLE depends on how hard it is to remove a further electron, i.e. on the third ionisation enthalpy.

Moving from Sc to Mn across the first half of the series, each added electron enters the inner \(3d\) subshell while the nuclear charge rises by one unit each time. A \(3d\) electron shields another \(3d\) electron poorly, so the effective nuclear charge acting on the \(3d\) electrons increases steadily and they are held progressively more tightly.

Removing a third electron therefore becomes harder and harder, and the tendency to go beyond \(+2\) falls away. So the \(+2\) state becomes more and more stable with increasing atomic number: Sc practically never shows \(+2\); \(\text{Ti}^{2+}\), \(\text{V}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) exist but are strongly reducing (they are readily oxidised to \(+3\)); by manganese, \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) is the most stable state of the element, helped further by its half-filled \(3d^{5}\) configuration.

The electronic configuration decides the stability of an oxidation state to a considerable extent, but it is not the only factor.

Where it clearly does decide: states that give an empty (\(d^{0}\)), exactly half-filled (\(d^{5}\)) or completely filled (\(d^{10}\)) \(3d\) subshell are unusually stable —

- \(d^{0}\): \(\text{Sc}^{3+}\) and \(\text{Ti}^{4+}\) are the only important states of those metals;
- \(d^{5}\): \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) is the most stable state of manganese, and \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) is more stable than \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\);
- \(d^{10}\): \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) is the only state of zinc, and \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) owes its existence in solids to it.

The number of electrons available also sets the ceiling: the maximum state of reasonable stability equals the sum of the \(s\) and \(d\) electrons up to manganese — \(\text{Ti}^{\text{IV}}\text{O}_2\), \(\text{V}^{\text{V}}\text{O}_2^{+}\), \(\text{Cr}^{\text{VI}}\text{O}_4^{2-}\), \(\text{Mn}^{\text{VII}}\text{O}_4^{-}\) — after which higher states become abruptly less stable.

Where configuration alone is NOT enough: \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Mn}^{3+}\) both have \(d^{4}\), yet the first is strongly reducing and the second strongly oxidising. Explaining that needs crystal-field stabilisation, ionisation enthalpies and hydration enthalpies as well. Similarly \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) has the ideal \(d^{10}\) configuration but still disproportionates in water, because the hydration enthalpy of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) overrides it.

So configuration gives a good first prediction, and the thermodynamic terms decide the borderline cases.

The available oxidation states are found by adding the \(4s^{2}\) electrons to the stated \(d\) electrons and asking which of the resulting states leaves a stable configuration.

\(3d^{3}\) — this is vanadium (\([\text{Ar}]3d^{3}4s^{2}\)). It can use up to five electrons, so it shows \(+2, +3, +4\) and \(+5\). The stable states in aqueous solution are \(+4\) (as \(\text{VO}^{2+}\)) and \(+5\) (as \(\text{VO}_2^{+}\)); \(\text{V}^{2+}\) is strongly reducing.

\(3d^{5}\) — this is manganese (\([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{2}\)). It shows \(+2\) through \(+7\). The most stable is \(+2\), because \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) retains the half-filled \(3d^{5}\) subshell; \(+4\) (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) and \(+7\) (\(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\)) are also well characterised.

\(3d^{8}\) — this is nickel (\([\text{Ar}]3d^{8}4s^{2}\)). Beyond the two \(4s\) electrons the \(3d\) electrons are held too tightly to be removed easily, so the stable state is \(+2\).

\(3d^{4}\) — NO neutral atom of the first series has this ground-state configuration, because chromium adopts \([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}\) in preference to \(3d^{4}4s^{2}\) for the extra stability of the half-filled subshell. A \(3d^{4}\) species therefore arises only as an ion, \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) or \(\text{Mn}^{3+}\), and neither is stable — \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) is strongly reducing (it goes to \(d^{3}\)) and \(\text{Mn}^{3+}\) strongly oxidising (it goes to \(d^{5}\)). Taking the atom as chromium, the stable state is \(+3\).

Stable states: \(3d^{3} \rightarrow +4/+5\); \(3d^{5} \rightarrow +2\); \(3d^{8} \rightarrow +2\); \(3d^{4} \rightarrow +3\) (no such neutral atom exists).
_note: Part (d) is the awkward one: no first-series atom has a 3d(4) GROUND state, since Cr is 3d(5)4s(1). A key could reasonably answer this either as 'Cr, stable state +3' or as 'Cr(2+)/Mn(3+), both unstable'. Both readings are given above.

solution:
An oxometal anion reaches the metal's group number when every valence electron (\(3d\) plus \(4s\)) has been used in bonding to oxygen. Working out the oxidation number from the charge:

\(\text{VO}_4^{3-}\) (vanadate): \(x + 4(-2) = -3\), so \(x = +5\) — vanadium is in group 5.

\(\text{CrO}_4^{2-}\) (chromate): \(x + 4(-2) = -2\), so \(x = +6\) — chromium is in group 6. The dichromate ion \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\) also has Cr in \(+6\).

\(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\) (permanganate): \(x + 4(-2) = -1\), so \(x = +7\) — manganese is in group 7.

The oxometal anions are \(\text{VO}_4^{3-}\), \(\text{CrO}_4^{2-}\) (and \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\)) and \(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\). Beyond group 7 the group oxidation state is no longer attainable, because the \(3d\) electrons become too tightly held.

Lanthanoid contraction is the steady, cumulative decrease in atomic and ionic radii of the lanthanoids with increasing atomic number, from La to Lu.

Cause: as we move along the series each added electron enters an inner \(4f\) orbital while the nuclear charge rises by one unit. The shielding of one \(4f\) electron by another is very imperfect — considerably poorer than that of one \(d\) electron by another — so the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons increases steadily and the whole \(4f^{n}\) shell shrinks.

Consequences:

1. The second and third transition series have almost identical sizes (Zr \(160\,\text{pm}\), Hf \(159\,\text{pm}\)), because the contraction cancels the expected increase on going from \(4d\) to \(5d\). Pairs such as Zr-Hf, Nb-Ta and Mo-W therefore have very similar physical and chemical properties and are extremely difficult to separate.

2. Because the size falls off, the density and the ionisation enthalpy of the \(5d\) elements are higher than expected.

3. The basicity of the lanthanoid hydroxides decreases steadily from \(\text{La(OH)}_3\) to \(\text{Lu(OH)}_3\), since the smaller, more polarising \(\text{Ln}^{3+}\) holds the hydroxide more covalently.

4. The size difference between successive lanthanoids is so small that separating the individual elements is very difficult, and their chemistry is remarkably uniform.

The difference lies in WHICH shell receives the differentiating electron.

Transition elements: the last electron enters the INNER \((n-1)d\) subshell, giving the general configuration

\((n-1)d^{1-10}\,ns^{1-2}\)

so the \(d\) subshell is incompletely filled either in the atom or in one of its stable ions. The penultimate shell is thus being built up while the outermost shell keeps one or two electrons.

Non-transition elements: the last electron enters the OUTERMOST shell, giving

\(ns^{1-2}\) for the \(s\)-block and \(ns^{2}np^{1-6}\) for the \(p\)-block

with no partly filled \(d\) subshell at all — the \((n-1)d\) level is either empty or completely filled.

The consequences follow directly: because the outermost shell of a transition element stays essentially the same across a series while an inner shell fills, the members of one horizontal row resemble one another closely, whereas non-transition elements change sharply along a period. And the absence of partly filled \(d\) orbitals is why non-transition elements are generally colourless, diamagnetic and show oxidation states differing by two rather than by one.

The characteristic and by far the commonest oxidation state of the lanthanoids is \(+3\); every member of the series shows it, and \(\text{Ln}^{3+}\) is what dominates their aqueous chemistry. It arises from the loss of the two \(6s\) electrons together with one \(5d\) (or \(4f\)) electron.

In addition a few members show:

\(+2\) — Sm, Eu and Yb (and Tm in the solid state);

\(+4\) — Ce, Pr, Nd, Tb and Dy, though only \(\text{Ce}^{4+}\) is important in solution.

These departures occur where the extra (or fewer) electrons lead to an empty, exactly half-filled or completely filled \(4f\) subshell: \(\text{Ce}^{4+}\) is \(4f^{0}\), \(\text{Tb}^{4+}\) and \(\text{Eu}^{2+}\) are \(4f^{7}\), and \(\text{Yb}^{2+}\) is \(4f^{14}\).

The non-\(+3\) states are correspondingly reactive in the direction that restores \(+3\): \(\text{Ce}^{4+}\) is a good oxidising agent and \(\text{Eu}^{2+}\) a good reducing agent.

(i) Paramagnetic behaviour. Transition metal atoms and most of their ions have unpaired electrons in the \((n-1)d\) orbitals. Each unpaired electron has a spin magnetic moment, and a substance containing them is drawn into an applied magnetic field. The moment follows the spin-only formula \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\text{BM}\), so it rises with the number of unpaired electrons and is zero for \(d^{0}\) and \(d^{10}\) ions such as \(\text{Sc}^{3+}\) and \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\), which are diamagnetic.

(ii) High enthalpies of atomisation. Metallic bonding here uses the \((n-1)d\) electrons in addition to the \(ns\) electrons, so a large number of electrons per atom is involved in binding the lattice. The greater the number of unpaired \(d\) electrons, the stronger the interatomic interaction, and the values pass through a maximum near the middle of each series. This also gives them high melting points and low volatility.

(iii) Coloured compounds. The five \(d\) orbitals are no longer degenerate once ligands surround the metal ion; they split into two sets. In an ion with a partly filled \(d\) subshell an electron can be promoted from the lower to the higher set (a \(d\)-\(d\) transition). The energy gap corresponds to a frequency in the visible region, so that light is absorbed and the compound shows the COMPLEMENTARY colour. Ions with \(d^{0}\) or \(d^{10}\) have no such transition available and are colourless — \(\text{Sc}^{3+}\), \(\text{Ti}^{4+}\), \(\text{Cu}^{+}\), \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\). The colour also depends on the ligand, since the ligand fixes the size of the gap.

(iv) Catalytic activity. Two properties are responsible. First, variable oxidation states let the metal accept and donate electrons, forming unstable intermediates with the reactants and providing a reaction path of lower activation energy — as with \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) catalysing the iodide-persulphate reaction, or \(\text{V}_2\text{O}_5\) in the Contact process. Second, at a solid surface the partly filled \(d\) orbitals can form weak bonds to reactant molecules, adsorbing and concentrating them and weakening their bonds — as with finely divided iron in the Haber process or nickel in hydrogenation.

Interstitial compounds are formed when small non-metal atoms — hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen or boron — become trapped in the interstices (the voids between the metal atoms) of a metal lattice. Examples: \(\text{TiC}\), \(\text{Mn}_4\text{N}\), \(\text{Fe}_3\text{H}\), \(\text{VH}_{0.56}\) and \(\text{TiH}_{1.7}\).

They are typically NON-STOICHIOMETRIC, so their formulae are not whole-number ratios and do not correspond to any normal valence of the metal; they are neither typically ionic nor typically covalent.

Why transition metals form them so readily: the transition metals have large atoms packed in lattices that leave interstitial holes of just the right size to accept H, C, N or B, and their metallic bonding is strong enough that inserting a small atom does not disrupt the lattice.

Characteristic properties: they have very high melting points, often higher than the pure metal; they are extremely hard (some metal borides approach diamond in hardness); they retain metallic conductivity; and they are chemically inert. The hardness of steel and cast iron over pure iron comes from exactly this — carbon occupying the interstices of the iron lattice.

The two differ in the SIZE OF THE STEP between successive oxidation states.

Transition metals: successive oxidation states differ by UNITY, because the \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) orbitals are close in energy and the electrons can be removed or shared one at a time. Thus vanadium gives \(\text{V}^{\text{II}}\), \(\text{V}^{\text{III}}\), \(\text{V}^{\text{IV}}\) and \(\text{V}^{\text{V}}\), and manganese runs through every state from \(+2\) to \(+7\).

Non-transition metals: oxidation states normally differ by TWO. The \(ns^{2}\) pair tends to be retained as a pair (the inert pair effect), so the element either keeps it or loses it entirely. Thus tin gives \(\text{Sn}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Sn}^{4+}\) but nothing between, lead gives \(\text{Pb}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Pb}^{4+}\), and thallium gives \(\text{Tl}^{+}\) and \(\text{Tl}^{3+}\).

A second contrast, in the group direction: among the \(p\)-block the LOWER state is favoured by the heavier members (the inert pair effect again), whereas in the \(d\)-block the opposite holds — the higher state is more stable for the heavier member. \(\text{Mo(VI)}\) and \(\text{W(VI)}\) are more stable than \(\text{Cr(VI)}\), which is why dichromate in acid is a strong oxidising agent while \(\text{MoO}_3\) and \(\text{WO}_3\) are not.

Preparation of potassium dichromate from chromite ore, \(\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4\), in three stages.

Stage 1 — conversion of the ore to chromate. The finely powdered ore is fused with sodium (or potassium) carbonate in free access of air:

\(4\,\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4 + 8\,\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 7\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 8\,\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4 + 2\,\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 8\,\text{CO}_2\)

The yellow sodium chromate is leached out with water and filtered from the insoluble \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\).

Stage 2 — acidification to the dichromate. The yellow solution is acidified with sulphuric acid, from which orange sodium dichromate, \(\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\), can be crystallised:

\(2\,\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4 + 2\,\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\,\text{Na}^{+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Stage 3 — conversion to the potassium salt. Sodium dichromate is treated with potassium chloride:

\(\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\,\text{KCl} \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\,\text{NaCl}\)

Potassium dichromate is much the less soluble of the two, so orange crystals of \(\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\) separate out on cooling.

Effect of increasing pH. Chromate and dichromate exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium. Increasing the pH (adding alkali) converts the orange dichromate into the yellow chromate:

\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 2\,\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow 2\,\text{CrO}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The change is reversed on lowering the pH again:

\(2\,\text{CrO}_4^{2-} + 2\,\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

So raising the pH turns the solution from orange to yellow. The oxidation state of chromium stays \(+6\) throughout — only the degree of condensation of the tetrahedral \(\text{CrO}_4\) units changes. Note also that the oxidising power is lost on doing so: dichromate is a strong oxidant only in acidic solution.

In acidic solution the dichromate ion is a powerful oxidising agent, chromium being reduced from \(+6\) to \(+3\) and the orange solution turning green:

\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\,\text{H}^{+} + 6\,e^{-} \rightarrow 2\,\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(E^{\circ} = +1.33\,\text{V}\)

Since six electrons are accepted, each half-reaction below is scaled to supply six.

(i) With iodide — iodide is oxidised to iodine:

\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\,\text{H}^{+} + 6\,\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2\,\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\,\text{I}_2\)

(ii) With iron(II) solution — iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III):

\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\,\text{H}^{+} + 6\,\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\,\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + 6\,\text{Fe}^{3+}\)

(iii) With \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) — sulphide sulphur is oxidised to free sulphur, which appears as a milky precipitate:

\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 8\,\text{H}^{+} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightarrow 2\,\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\,\text{S}\)

(Here three of the fourteen \(\text{H}^{+}\) required by the half-reaction are furnished by the \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) itself, which is why only eight appear on the left.)

It is the reaction in (ii) that makes \(\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\) a primary standard for the volumetric estimation of iron(II).

Preparation of potassium permanganate from pyrolusite, \(\text{MnO}_2\), in two stages.

Stage 1 — oxidation of the ore to manganate. \(\text{MnO}_2\) is fused with an alkali metal hydroxide in the presence of air or an oxidising agent such as \(\text{KNO}_3\), giving the dark green potassium manganate:

\(2\,\text{MnO}_2 + 4\,\text{KOH} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\,\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Stage 2 — oxidation of manganate to permanganate. This is done commercially by electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution, at the anode:

\(\text{MnO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{MnO}_4^{-} + e^{-}\)

Alternatively the green manganate disproportionates on acidification:

\(3\,\text{MnO}_4^{2-} + 4\,\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2\,\text{MnO}_4^{-} + \text{MnO}_2 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The purple \(\text{KMnO}_4\) is then crystallised out.

Reactions of acidified permanganate. In acid solution manganese is reduced from \(+7\) to \(+2\), five electrons being accepted and the purple colour discharged:

\(\text{MnO}_4^{-} + 8\,\text{H}^{+} + 5\,e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(E^{\circ} = +1.51\,\text{V}\)

(i) With iron(II) ions — oxidised to iron(III):

\(\text{MnO}_4^{-} + 8\,\text{H}^{+} + 5\,\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + 5\,\text{Fe}^{3+}\)

(ii) With sulphur dioxide — oxidised to sulphate:

\(2\,\text{MnO}_4^{-} + 5\,\text{SO}_2 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\,\text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\,\text{SO}_4^{2-} + 4\,\text{H}^{+}\)

(iii) With oxalic acid — the oxalate is oxidised to carbon dioxide (the solution is warmed to about \(333\,\text{K}\)):

\(2\,\text{MnO}_4^{-} + 16\,\text{H}^{+} + 5\,\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2\,\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + 10\,\text{CO}_2\)

All three are used volumetrically, permanganate acting as its own indicator.

The two sets of data answer two different questions: the \(\text{M}^{3+}/\text{M}^{2+}\) values say how readily the \(+3\) ion is REDUCED, and the \(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M}\) values say how readily the METAL is oxidised.

(i) Stability of \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) compared with \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) and \(\text{Mn}^{3+}\).

A large positive \(E^{\circ}(\text{M}^{3+}/\text{M}^{2+})\) means the \(+3\) ion is easily reduced to \(+2\), i.e. it is a strong oxidising agent and therefore NOT stable in acid solution.

\(\text{Mn}^{3+}/\text{Mn}^{2+} = +1.5\,\text{V}\) — strongly positive, so \(\text{Mn}^{3+}\) is very readily reduced and is the least stable. (It reverts to the half-filled \(d^{5}\) \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\).)

\(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+} = +0.8\,\text{V}\) — positive but much less so, so \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) is a moderate oxidising agent and of intermediate stability.

\(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+} = -0.4\,\text{V}\) — NEGATIVE, so \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) is not reduced at all readily; on the contrary \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) is spontaneously oxidised to it. \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) is much the most stable, helped by its \(t_{2g}^{3}\) configuration.

Stability of the \(+3\) ion in acid solution: \(\text{Cr}^{3+} > \text{Fe}^{3+} > \text{Mn}^{3+}\).

(ii) Ease with which the metal is oxidised.

The more NEGATIVE \(E^{\circ}(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M})\), the greater the tendency of the metal to go into solution as \(\text{M}^{2+}\):

\(\text{Mn}\;(-1.2\,\text{V}) < \text{Cr}\;(-0.9\,\text{V}) < \text{Fe}\;(-0.4\,\text{V})\)

so the ease of oxidation runs \(\text{Mn} > \text{Cr} > \text{Fe}\).

Iron is therefore oxidised LESS readily than either chromium or manganese metal. The unusually negative value for manganese reflects the extra stability of the \(d^{5}\) \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) ion that is formed.

\(\text{Ti}^{3+}\): \([\text{Ar}]3d^{1}\) — partly filled, COLOURED (purple).

\(\text{V}^{3+}\): \([\text{Ar}]3d^{2}\) — partly filled, COLOURED (green).

\(\text{Cu}^{+}\): \([\text{Ar}]3d^{10}\) — completely filled, no \(d\)-\(d\) transition possible, COLOURLESS.

\(\text{Sc}^{3+}\): \([\text{Ar}]3d^{0}\) — no \(d\) electron to promote, COLOURLESS.

\(\text{Mn}^{2+}\): \([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}\) — partly filled, COLOURED, but only a very pale pink, because for a high-spin \(d^{5}\) ion every \(d\)-\(d\) transition also requires a spin flip and is therefore doubly forbidden and very weak.

Coloured: \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\), \(\text{V}^{3+}\), \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\), \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\), \(\text{Co}^{2+}\). Colourless: \(\text{Cu}^{+}\), \(\text{Sc}^{3+}\).

The \(+2\) state corresponds to the loss of the two \(4s\) electrons, and its stability is governed by how tightly the remaining \(3d\) electrons are held — that is, by the third ionisation enthalpy — and by the stability of the resulting \(d^{n}\) configuration.

Across the series the effective nuclear charge on the \(3d\) electrons rises steadily (a \(3d\) electron screens another \(3d\) electron poorly), so removing a third electron becomes progressively harder and the \(+2\) state becomes progressively more stable:

- Sc: \(\text{Sc}^{2+}\) is virtually unknown; scandium goes straight to the \(d^{0}\) \(\text{Sc}^{3+}\).
- Ti, V, Cr: \(\text{Ti}^{2+}\), \(\text{V}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) exist but are strong REDUCING agents — they liberate hydrogen from dilute acid, e.g. \(2\,\text{Cr}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\,\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\,\text{Cr}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + \text{H}_2(\text{g})\).
- Mn: \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) is the most stable state of manganese, its \(3d^{5}\) half-filled subshell giving it extra stability.
- Fe, Co, Ni, Cu: \(+2\) is the common and stable state; \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) is still mildly reducing (it goes to the \(d^{5}\) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\)), while \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) are quite stable.
- Zn: \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) (\(3d^{10}\)) is the ONLY state zinc shows.

The trend is mirrored in the electrode potentials, \(E^{\circ}(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M})\) becoming generally less negative from Ti to Cu (reaching \(+0.34\,\text{V}\) for copper), which tracks the increasing sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies. Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than the trend predicts — for Mn and Zn because of the extra stability of the \(d^{5}\) and \(d^{10}\) ions formed, and for Ni because of its exceptionally negative hydration enthalpy.

Summary: \(+2\) is unimportant at the start of the series, becomes reducing but real for Ti-Cr, and is the dominant stable state from Mn onwards.

(i) Electronic configuration. Lanthanoids: \([\text{Xe}]4f^{1-14}5d^{0-1}6s^{2}\). Actinoids: \([\text{Rn}]5f^{1-14}6d^{0-1}7s^{2}\). In both the differentiating electron enters an inner \(f\) subshell, but the actinoid configurations are far less regular, because the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) levels lie much closer together in energy than the corresponding lanthanoid levels.

(ii) Atomic and ionic sizes. Both series show a steady contraction with increasing atomic number, caused by the imperfect shielding of one \(f\) electron by another. But the actinoid contraction is GREATER from element to element, because \(5f\) orbitals are more diffuse and shield the nuclear charge even less effectively than \(4f\) orbitals do.

(iii) Oxidation state. The lanthanoids are dominated by \(+3\), with only occasional \(+2\) (Sm, Eu, Yb) and \(+4\) (Ce, Tb) states, and these occur where an empty, half-filled or full \(4f\) subshell results. The actinoids show a much WIDER range — \(+3\) is still the commonest, but \(+4, +5, +6\) and even \(+7\) occur (Th is mainly \(+4\); U shows \(+3\) to \(+6\); Np and Pu reach \(+7\)). The reason is again the near-degeneracy of the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) levels, which makes more electrons available for bonding, together with the lower ionisation enthalpies of the early actinoids.

(iv) Chemical reactivity. The lanthanoids are reactive electropositive metals that tarnish in air and react with water, but they behave very uniformly and predictably. The actinoids are HIGHLY reactive, especially when finely divided: boiling water gives a mixture of oxide and hydride, they combine with most non-metals at moderate temperature, and hydrochloric acid attacks them all — although nitric acid passivates most of them by forming a protective oxide layer, and alkalies have no action. In addition all the actinoids are radioactive, which makes their study experimentally difficult; behaviour resembling the lanthanoids is not really evident until the second half of the actinoid series.

(i) Both are \(d^{4}\), so the difference lies entirely in what each becomes on gaining or losing one electron.

\(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) is oxidised: \(d^{4} \rightarrow d^{3}\). In an octahedral aqueous field \(d^{3}\) is \(t_{2g}^{3}\), a half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level with the largest crystal-field stabilisation energy available to a high-spin ion. The strong drive to reach it makes \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) a powerful REDUCING agent.

\(\text{Mn}^{3+}\) is reduced: \(d^{4} \rightarrow d^{5}\), the exactly half-filled \(3d\) subshell with its large exchange energy. The strong drive to reach that makes manganese(III) a powerful OXIDISING agent.

(ii) Cobalt(II) is the stable state in plain aqueous solution, where the ligand is water. But a strong-field (complexing) ligand such as \(\text{NH}_3\) or \(\text{CN}^{-}\) produces a large splitting \(\Delta_o\), and cobalt(III) is \(d^{6}\), which under a large \(\Delta_o\) becomes low-spin \(t_{2g}^{6}\) — a completely filled, spherically symmetrical \(t_{2g}\) set with an exceptionally large crystal-field stabilisation energy. Cobalt(II), \(d^{7}\), cannot gain nearly as much. The complexing agent therefore stabilises the \(+3\) state far more than the \(+2\) state, driving \(E^{\circ}(\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+})\) down from about \(+1.8\,\text{V}\) in water to roughly \(+0.1\,\text{V}\) in ammonia, so cobalt(II) is then oxidised by air.

(iii) An ion with a \(d^{1}\) configuration has a single, loosely held \(d\) electron and lies just one electron away from the \(d^{0}\) noble-gas configuration. Losing it costs little and gains the stability of the empty subshell, so \(d^{1}\) ions are readily oxidised and are unstable — \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\) passes to \(\text{Ti}^{4+}\) and \(\text{V}^{4+}\) to \(\text{V}^{5+}\), so both act as reducing agents.

Disproportionation is a reaction in which ONE species in a particular oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised AND reduced, giving products in a higher and a lower oxidation state. It happens when that intermediate state is less stable than the two states flanking it.

Two examples in aqueous solution:

1. Manganate(VI) in acidic solution goes to manganese(VII) and manganese(IV) — the green solution turns purple with a brown precipitate:

\(3\,\text{Mn}^{\text{VI}}\text{O}_4^{2-} + 4\,\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2\,\text{Mn}^{\text{VII}}\text{O}_4^{-} + \text{Mn}^{\text{IV}}\text{O}_2 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

2. Copper(I) goes to copper(II) and copper metal:

\(2\,\text{Cu}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Cu(s)}\)

Here the very large hydration enthalpy of the small, doubly charged \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) more than pays for the second ionisation enthalpy of copper, which is why copper(I) cannot exist in water.

Copper, \(Z = 29\).

Copper is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}\). It is the only member of the first transition series with a single electron outside a completely filled \(3d\) subshell, so losing just that one \(4s\) electron gives

\(\text{Cu}^{+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{10}\)

which is a stable, completely filled configuration. No other first-series metal can reach a \(d^{10}\) ion by losing only one electron, so none of them shows \(+1\) with any frequency.

Copper(I) is nevertheless confined to the solid state and to insoluble or complexed species — \(\text{Cu}_2\text{O}\), CuCl, CuI — because in water \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) disproportionates to \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) and Cu.

For a gaseous ion the \(4s\) electrons are lost first, then the \(3d\); the remaining \(d\) electrons are distributed over the five degenerate \(3d\) orbitals by Hund's rule (a free gaseous ion has no ligand field, so it is always high spin).

\(\text{Mn}^{3+}\): Mn is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{2}\), so \(\text{Mn}^{3+} = 3d^{4}\) — four unpaired electrons.

\(\text{Cr}^{3+}\): Cr is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}\), so \(\text{Cr}^{3+} = 3d^{3}\) — three unpaired electrons.

\(\text{V}^{3+}\): V is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{3}4s^{2}\), so \(\text{V}^{3+} = 3d^{2}\) — two unpaired electrons.

\(\text{Ti}^{3+}\): Ti is \([\text{Ar}]3d^{2}4s^{2}\), so \(\text{Ti}^{3+} = 3d^{1}\) — one unpaired electron.

Most stable in aqueous solution: \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\). In the octahedral field of the six water molecules its \(d^{3}\) configuration becomes \(t_{2g}^{3}\), a half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level which carries the maximum crystal-field stabilisation energy attainable by a high-spin ion. By contrast \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\) and \(\text{V}^{3+}\) are readily oxidised towards the \(d^{0}\) state, and \(\text{Mn}^{3+}\) is strongly oxidising and reverts to the \(d^{5}\) \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\).

(i) The lowest oxide is basic, the highest amphoteric or acidic.

As the oxidation number of the metal rises, the cation becomes smaller and more highly charged, hence far more polarising. It distorts the oxide ion strongly, so the M-O bond loses ionic character and becomes largely covalent; a covalent oxide reacts with water to give an oxoacid rather than a hydroxide.

Examples: for manganese, MnO (Mn(II)) is basic, \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_3\) is weakly basic, \(\text{MnO}_2\) is amphoteric and \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7\) is acidic — it is a covalent green oil giving \(\text{HMnO}_4\). For chromium, CrO is basic, \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3\) amphoteric and \(\text{CrO}_3\) acidic, giving \(\text{H}_2\text{CrO}_4\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\).

(ii) The highest oxidation state appears in oxides and fluorides.

Oxygen and fluorine are the smallest and most electronegative elements, so they are the strongest oxidising partners available, and their small size lets a large number of them surround one metal atom (a high coordination number). Oxygen has the further advantage of forming \(p\pi\)-\(d\pi\) MULTIPLE bonds to the metal, so it stabilises a very high state with fewer atoms.

Examples: \(\text{V}_2\text{O}_5\) (V(V)), \(\text{CrO}_3\) (Cr(VI)), \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7\) (Mn(VII)), \(\text{OsF}_6\) and \(\text{OsO}_4\) (Os(VIII)). The superiority of oxygen shows up directly: the highest manganese FLUORIDE is only \(\text{MnF}_4\), whereas the highest oxide is \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7\).

(iii) The highest oxidation state is exhibited in oxoanions.

In an oxoanion the metal is surrounded by several oxygen atoms, each able to form the multiple bonds described above, and the resulting negative charge is delocalised over them. This combination lets the metal reach a higher state than any simple binary compound allows, and the tetrahedral \([\text{MO}_4]^{n-}\) ion is the usual form.

Examples: \(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\) (Mn(VII)), \(\text{CrO}_4^{2-}\) and \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\) (Cr(VI)), \(\text{VO}_4^{3-}\) (V(V)), \(\text{FeO}_4^{2-}\) (Fe(VI), the highest state iron reaches at all).

(i) \(\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\) from chromite ore, \(\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4\):

Step 1 — fuse the powdered ore with sodium carbonate in free access of air to convert chromium(III) to chromate:

\(4\,\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4 + 8\,\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 7\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 8\,\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4 + 2\,\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 8\,\text{CO}_2\)

Step 2 — extract with water, filter off the insoluble \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\), and acidify the yellow chromate solution with sulphuric acid to crystallise orange sodium dichromate:

\(2\,\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4 + 2\,\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\,\text{Na}^{+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Step 3 — treat the sodium dichromate with potassium chloride; \(\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\) is far less soluble and crystallises out:

\(\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\,\text{KCl} \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\,\text{NaCl}\)

(ii) \(\text{KMnO}_4\) from pyrolusite ore, \(\text{MnO}_2\):

Step 1 — fuse the ore with potassium hydroxide in the presence of air (or an oxidising agent such as \(\text{KNO}_3\)) to give the dark green manganate:

\(2\,\text{MnO}_2 + 4\,\text{KOH} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\,\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Step 2 — oxidise manganate to permanganate, industrially by electrolytic oxidation of the alkaline solution:

\(\text{MnO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{MnO}_4^{-} + e^{-}\)

(In the laboratory the same conversion is achieved by acidifying, when the manganate disproportionates: \(3\,\text{MnO}_4^{2-} + 4\,\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2\,\text{MnO}_4^{-} + \text{MnO}_2 + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\).)

Step 3 — concentrate and crystallise the purple \(\text{KMnO}_4\).

An alloy is a homogeneous solid solution obtained by melting together two or more metals (or a metal with a non-metal) and allowing the mixture to solidify. Transition metals alloy with one another particularly readily, because their atomic radii are so similar that one metal can replace another in the crystal lattice without disturbing it.

An important alloy containing lanthanoid metals is MISCHMETALL. Its composition is roughly \(95\%\) lanthanoid metal and \(5\%\) iron, together with traces of S, C, Ca and Al.

Uses: a good deal of mischmetall goes into magnesium-based alloys, from which bullets, shells and lighter flints are made. More broadly, the best single use of the lanthanoids is in producing alloy steels for plates and pipes, where they act as scavengers for sulphur and oxygen.

Inner transition elements are those in which the last electron enters an \((n-2)f\) orbital — that is, the second-from-outermost shell is being filled. They constitute the \(f\)-block: the lanthanoids (\(4f\), Ce to Lu, following lanthanum) and the actinoids (\(5f\), Th to Lr, following actinium), and are placed in a separate panel at the foot of the periodic table. Their general configuration is \((n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^{2}\).

Taking the given atomic numbers in turn:

\(29\) — copper, \([\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}\): a \(d\)-block element. NO.

\(59\) — praseodymium, \([\text{Xe}]4f^{3}6s^{2}\): a lanthanoid. YES.

\(74\) — tungsten, \([\text{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^{4}6s^{2}\): a \(d\)-block element of the third transition series. NO.

\(95\) — americium, \([\text{Rn}]5f^{7}7s^{2}\): an actinoid. YES.

\(102\) — nobelium, \([\text{Rn}]5f^{14}7s^{2}\): an actinoid. YES.

\(104\) — rutherfordium, \([\text{Rn}]5f^{14}6d^{2}7s^{2}\): the \(5f\) shell is complete and the \(6d\) is filling, so it is a \(d\)-block (fourth transition series) element. NO.

The inner transition elements are those with \(Z = 59, 95\) and \(102\).

The actinoid series runs from thorium (\(Z = 90\)) to lawrencium (\(Z = 103\)), so the last element is LAWRENCIUM, Lr.

Its electronic configuration is

\(\text{Lr} = [\text{Rn}]5f^{14}6d^{1}7s^{2}\)

Possible oxidation state: \(+3\) only. The \(5f\) subshell is completely filled and therefore very stable and unavailable for bonding, so the only electrons that can be lost are the single \(6d\) electron and the two \(7s\) electrons — exactly three. Losing them leaves the stable \([\text{Rn}]5f^{14}\) core.

Lawrencium is thus the actinoid analogue of lutetium, which for the same reason shows only \(+3\).

Cerium has \(Z = 58\), and the neutral atom is

\(\text{Ce} = [\text{Xe}]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}\)

Forming \(\text{Ce}^{3+}\) removes the two \(6s\) electrons and the \(5d\) electron, leaving

\(\text{Ce}^{3+} = [\text{Xe}]4f^{1}\)

Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity requires that electrons occupy the seven degenerate \(4f\) orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing occurs. With only one \(4f\) electron present it therefore sits alone in one \(4f\) orbital and remains unpaired:

\(n = 1\)

Spin-only magnetic moment:

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3}\)

\(\mu = 1.73\,\text{BM}\)

(i) Electronic configuration. Lanthanoids: \([\text{Xe}]4f^{1-14}5d^{0-1}6s^{2}\). Actinoids: \([\text{Rn}]5f^{1-14}6d^{0-1}7s^{2}\). Both fill an inner \(f\) subshell, but the actinoid configurations are much more irregular, because the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) levels lie close together in energy whereas the \(4f\) level is well separated and deeply buried.

(ii) Oxidation states. The lanthanoids are dominated by \(+3\), with \(+2\) and \(+4\) appearing only for the few elements where an empty, half-filled or full \(4f\) subshell results (\(\text{Ce}^{4+}\), \(\text{Tb}^{4+}\), \(\text{Eu}^{2+}\), \(\text{Yb}^{2+}\)). The actinoids show a far wider range: \(+3\) is still common but \(+4, +5, +6\) and \(+7\) all occur (Th mainly \(+4\), U up to \(+6\), Np and Pu up to \(+7\)), because the near-degenerate \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) electrons are all available for bonding and the early actinoids have lower ionisation enthalpies.

(iii) Chemical reactivity. The lanthanoids are reactive electropositive metals but behave very uniformly, so the whole series is chemically alike and hard to separate. The actinoids are far more reactive, especially when finely divided: boiling water gives a mixture of oxide and hydride, they combine with most non-metals at moderate temperature, hydrochloric acid attacks them all, while nitric acid passivates most of them through a protective oxide film and alkalies do not attack them. Every actinoid is also radioactive, which makes their chemistry experimentally far harder to study.

\(Z = 61\) — promethium, a lanthanoid:

\(\text{Pm} = [\text{Xe}]4f^{5}6s^{2}\)

\(Z = 91\) — protactinium, an actinoid. Here the \(6d\) and \(5f\) levels are so close that one electron stays in \(6d\):

\(\text{Pa} = [\text{Rn}]5f^{2}6d^{1}7s^{2}\)

\(Z = 101\) — mendelevium, an actinoid of the second half of the series, where the \(5f\) level has dropped well below the \(6d\):

\(\text{Md} = [\text{Rn}]5f^{13}7s^{2}\)

\(Z = 109\) — meitnerium, a \(d\)-block element of the fourth transition series (the \(5f\) shell is already complete):

\(\text{Mt} = [\text{Rn}]5f^{14}6d^{7}7s^{2}\)

(i) Electronic configurations. The three series are \(3d^{1-10}4s^{1-2}\), \(4d^{1-10}5s^{0-2}\) and \(5d^{1-10}6s^{1-2}\). Irregularities are far commoner in the \(4d\) and \(5d\) series than in the \(3d\), because the \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) energies lie closer together in the heavier members — hence Nb \(4d^{4}5s^{1}\), Ru \(4d^{7}5s^{1}\), Rh \(4d^{8}5s^{1}\), Pd \(4d^{10}5s^{0}\) (no \(s\) electron at all) and Pt \(5d^{9}6s^{1}\).

(ii) Oxidation states. Down a group the HIGHER oxidation states become more stable, the opposite of the \(p\)-block. \(\text{Mo(VI)}\) and \(\text{W(VI)}\) are more stable than \(\text{Cr(VI)}\), which is why acidified dichromate is a strong oxidising agent while \(\text{MoO}_3\) and \(\text{WO}_3\) are not. The heavier members also reach states the \(3d\) series never attains — \(+8\) in \(\text{RuO}_4\) and \(\text{OsO}_4\). Correspondingly, the low oxidation states (\(+2, +3\)) that dominate the \(3d\) series are much less important for the \(4d\) and \(5d\) metals.

(iii) Ionisation enthalpies. There is no simple monotonic trend, but in general the \(5d\) elements have HIGHER ionisation enthalpies than the corresponding \(4d\) elements, because the lanthanoid contraction has pulled the \(5d\) atoms in to the same size while the nuclear charge is far larger, and the intervening \(4f\) electrons shield very poorly. This is a major reason why the \(5d\) metals (Pt, Au) are so noble.

(iv) Atomic sizes. Radii increase appreciably from the \(3d\) to the \(4d\) series, as expected on adding a shell. But the \(5d\) radii are virtually IDENTICAL to the \(4d\) ones — Zr \(160\,\text{pm}\) against Hf \(159\,\text{pm}\) — because the \(4f\) orbitals must be filled before the \(5d\) series begins, and the resulting lanthanoid contraction exactly compensates the expected increase.

The consequence of (iv) is that \(4d\)-\(5d\) congeners such as Zr-Hf, Nb-Ta and Mo-W have remarkably similar physical and chemical properties and are very difficult to separate — a resemblance much closer than the usual family relationship. The heavier members also have higher enthalpies of atomisation and show much more frequent metal-metal bonding in their compounds.

Water is a WEAK-field ligand, so all these hydrated octahedral ions are HIGH SPIN: the five \(3d\) orbitals split into a lower \(t_{2g}\) set of three and an upper \(e_g\) set of two, and because \(\Delta_o\) is smaller than the pairing energy the electrons occupy all five singly before any pairing occurs.

\(\text{Ti}^{2+}\): \(3d^{2}\) — \(t_{2g}^{2}e_g^{0}\), 2 unpaired

\(\text{V}^{2+}\): \(3d^{3}\) — \(t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{0}\), 3 unpaired

\(\text{Cr}^{3+}\): \(3d^{3}\) — \(t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{0}\), 3 unpaired

\(\text{Mn}^{2+}\): \(3d^{5}\) — \(t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}\), 5 unpaired

\(\text{Fe}^{2+}\): \(3d^{6}\) — \(t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}\), 4 unpaired

\(\text{Fe}^{3+}\): \(3d^{5}\) — \(t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}\), 5 unpaired

\(\text{Co}^{2+}\): \(3d^{7}\) — \(t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{2}\), 3 unpaired

\(\text{Ni}^{2+}\): \(3d^{8}\) — \(t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{2}\), 2 unpaired

\(\text{Cu}^{2+}\): \(3d^{9}\) — \(t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{3}\), 1 unpaired

The pattern is that the first five electrons go singly into \(t_{2g}\) then \(e_g\) (giving the maximum of five unpaired electrons at \(d^{5}\)), after which the sixth to ninth pair up in the \(t_{2g}\) set first and then in \(e_g\). These occupancies are what the observed magnetic moments of the hydrated ions confirm.

The statement is correct, and the differences are systematic rather than accidental.

Size. The \(3d\) atoms and ions are distinctly smaller than their heavier congeners. But the difference between the \(4d\) and \(5d\) members is negligible (Zr \(160\,\text{pm}\), Hf \(159\,\text{pm}\)) because of the lanthanoid contraction, so it is the FIRST series that stands apart while the other two resemble each other closely.

Oxidation states. The \(3d\) elements show many low oxidation states, \(+2\) and \(+3\) being characteristic, and their high oxidation states are strongly oxidising and hard to reach. The heavier elements reach high states easily and hold them stably: \(\text{Mo(VI)}\) and \(\text{W(VI)}\) are more stable than \(\text{Cr(VI)}\), and \(\text{RuO}_4\) and \(\text{OsO}_4\) reach \(+8\), which no \(3d\) element attains.

Enthalpy of atomisation and melting point. The \(4d\) and \(5d\) metals have appreciably higher enthalpies of atomisation than the corresponding \(3d\) metals, and correspondingly higher melting points — which is also why metal-metal bonding and cluster compounds are so much commoner among the heavy transition metals.

Magnetic and complexing behaviour. Because \(4d\) and \(5d\) orbitals are larger and more diffuse, they interact more strongly with ligands and give a much larger crystal-field splitting. Complexes of the \(3d\) metals are therefore usually HIGH-SPIN and paramagnetic, whereas those of the \(4d\) and \(5d\) metals are usually LOW-SPIN and often diamagnetic. The heavier metals also form more numerous and more stable complexes, and show higher coordination numbers.

Nobility. The high enthalpies of atomisation and ionisation enthalpies of the \(5d\) metals make them chemically inert — Pt, Ir and Au are noble, while the corresponding \(3d\) metals (Ni, Co, Cu) are reactive enough to dissolve in mineral acids.

So the first transition series, being the smallest and least strongly bonded, differs from the heavier series in size, in the stability of its higher oxidation states, in its atomisation enthalpies, and in the spin states and stability of its complexes.

The spin-only formula \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\text{BM}\) gives \(1.73, 2.83, 3.87, 4.90\) and \(5.92\,\text{BM}\) for \(n = 1\) to \(5\) unpaired electrons, so each measured moment can be read back as a value of \(n\), and from \(n\) we learn whether the ligand is weak- or strong-field.

\(\text{K}_4[\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]\), \(2.2\,\text{BM}\). The complex ion is \([\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}\); six \(\text{CN}^{-}\) contribute \(-6\), so manganese is \(+2\), i.e. \(3d^{5}\). A moment of \(2.2\) corresponds to ONE unpaired electron (spin-only \(1.73\)), not five. Cyanide is a strong-field ligand, so \(\Delta_o\) exceeds the pairing energy and the ion is LOW SPIN, \(t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}\), leaving a single unpaired electron. The excess over the spin-only value comes from a small residual orbital contribution.

\([\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\), \(5.3\,\text{BM}\). Iron is \(+2\), i.e. \(3d^{6}\). The value is close to \(4.90\), so there are FOUR unpaired electrons. Water is a weak-field ligand, so the ion is HIGH SPIN, \(t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}\).

\(\text{K}_2[\text{MnCl}_4]\), \(5.9\,\text{BM}\). The complex ion is \([\text{MnCl}_4]^{2-}\); four \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) contribute \(-4\), so manganese is again \(+2\), \(3d^{5}\). The value matches \(5.92\) almost exactly, so all FIVE electrons are unpaired. Chloride is a weak-field ligand and the four-coordinate geometry is tetrahedral, where the splitting is smaller still, so the ion is HIGH SPIN.

What can be inferred: the magnetic moment gives the number of unpaired electrons and hence the metal's \(d\)-configuration and spin state. Comparing the first and third entries is the instructive part — both are manganese(II), \(d^{5}\), yet one has one unpaired electron and the other five. The difference is entirely due to the ligand: \(\text{CN}^{-}\) is strong-field and forces pairing, \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) is weak-field and does not.
